question: The Power of Context
content: Environment acts as a silent driver of behavior. We tend to choose the options most visible and accessible in our surroundings.
description: A company redesigns its office cafeteria. They place salad ingredients at eye level in the first cooler, desserts in a separate corner behind a pillar, and remove trays so employees must carry each item individually. Salad sales increase 40%. Dessert sales drop 25%. Critics argue this is manipulative choice architecture that infringes on freedom. Proponents argue it preserves full choice while respecting how the brain actually works. Which reasoning best defends the design as ethical rather than manipulative?
options: The changes are ethical because salad is objectively healthier than dessert, and companies have a duty to promote health
The changes are ethical because every food option remains available with equal effort to access; no choice is removed or penalized
The changes are ethical because the company disclosed the redesign intent in a company-wide email before implementation
The changes are ethical because employees can still ask staff to retrieve any item from the back, preserving full access
answer: The changes are ethical because every food option remains available with equal effort to access; no choice is removed or penalized
explanation: Libertarian paternalism argues that environment design is ethical when it steers without restricting. All foods are equally available and equally priced. The design works with the brain's visual dominance (50% of neural resources) rather than against it. Employees remain free to walk to the dessert corner and carry it on a tray. The choice architecture merely changes what is noticed first, which compensates for the mismatch between evolved attention systems and modern food environments.

question: Visual Cues and Behavior
content: Half of the brain resources are dedicated to vision. Small changes in what you see lead to big shifts in what you do.
description: An office manager wants employees to drink more water without banning soda. What environmental change works best?
options: Send a company email about sugar dangers
Place water bottles at eye level in coolers and move sodas to the bottom
Increase the price of soda in the vending machine
Post posters of athletes drinking water
answer: Place water bottles at eye level in coolers and move sodas to the bottom
explanation: This is choice architecture. By placing the healthier option in the direct line of sight, the brain visual dominance drives better choices without banning anything.

question: Context is the Cue
content: Habits become tied to entire contexts, not just single triggers. The environment itself becomes the cue.
description: A person struggles to sleep because they often work on a laptop in bed. What is the recommended solution?
options: Buy a more comfortable pillow
Drink coffee earlier to be tired at night
Use the bed only for sleep and move all work to a desk
Set a timer to turn off the laptop at 10 PM
answer: Use the bed only for sleep and move all work to a desk
explanation: When contexts are mixed, cues become blurred. Dedicating the bed strictly to sleep makes the physical environment an unmistakable cue for rest.

question: The One Space One Use Rule
content: It is easier to build a new habit in a new context than to fight old cues in a familiar space.
description: Someone wants to write creatively but their gaming computer triggers the urge to play video games. What should they do?
options: Use willpower to ignore the games while writing
Delete all games every time they want to write
Find a specific corner of a library where they only write
Promise a gaming reward after finishing writing
answer: Find a specific corner of a library where they only write
explanation: Every space has associations based on past habits. Creating a writing-only zone builds a clean association where the environment itself triggers the writing mindset.

question: Environment Design for Consistency
content: Design your environment so that the cues for good habits are part of the path of least resistance.
description: Someone wants to practice guitar more often. Which setup is most effective?
options: Keep the guitar in its case inside a closet
Put the guitar on a stand in the middle of the living room
Store the guitar at a friend house to force travel
Rely on memory to take the guitar out when free
answer: Put the guitar on a stand in the middle of the living room
explanation: Out of sight, out of mind. Making the guitar a permanent visible fixture ensures the cue is constantly present, making it much more likely you will pick it up.

question: The Inversion: Make it Invisible
content: The most reliable way to break a bad habit is to remove its cue from your environment entirely.
description: Someone spends too much on impulse purchases through shopping apps. What is the most effective Make it Invisible strategy?
options: Delete the shopping apps from the phone entirely
Mute notifications but keep apps on the home screen
Promise to be more disciplined next time
Set a monthly budget on paper
answer: Delete the shopping apps from the phone entirely
explanation: If you do not see the app, you do not receive the cue to browse. Removing the trigger is more reliable than trying to resist temptation once it is in front of you.

question: Self-Control vs. Environment Design
content: Self-control is a short-term strategy. Environment design is a long-term solution because disciplined people avoid temptation rather than resist it.
description: Why is relying on willpower to resist junk food usually a failing strategy?
options: Because willpower is a fixed resource that never grows
Because you must exercise willpower every time you see the food, which is exhausting
Because junk food is biologically addictive
Because willpower only works for athletic people
answer: Because you must exercise willpower every time you see the food, which is exhausting
explanation: Willpower depletes. If junk food is on the counter, you must say no dozens of times daily. If you do not buy it, you only say no once at the store. Environment wins.

question: Stable Environments and Habit Change
content: A stable, predictable environment with consistent cues is the best foundation for reliable habits.
description: Someone wants to study daily for a certification. Which environment is most likely to produce a consistent study habit?
options: Study at a different coffee shop each day for variety
Study on the bed while the TV plays in the background
Use the same quiet library desk at the same time each day
Study at the dining table while family eats dinner
answer: Use the same quiet library desk at the same time each day
explanation: Consistency in location builds a strong association. Over time, simply sitting at that specific desk automatically triggers study mode because the cues are stable.

question: Hidden Cues of Consumption
content: Micro-cues like plate size or glass shape influence consumption without conscious awareness.
description: Someone wants to reduce alcohol at home. What is an effective Make it Invisible environmental change?
options: Buy smaller glasses for drinks
Store the alcohol in a high cabinet that requires a stool to reach
Read a book about the negative effects of alcohol
Make a pact with a friend to stop drinking
answer: Store the alcohol in a high cabinet that requires a stool to reach
explanation: Moving alcohol out of sight removes the visual cue, and adding friction by making it harder to reach stops the autopilot habit of pouring a drink.

question: Priming the Environment
content: Environmental priming means arranging your space in advance to make future good actions effortless.
description: Someone wants to exercise first thing in the morning. How can they prime the environment the night before?
options: Set three different alarms on the phone
Lay out workout clothes and shoes right next to the bed
Promise a big breakfast after the workout
Visualize how great they will look fit
answer: Lay out workout clothes and shoes right next to the bed
explanation: Laying out clothes makes the cue obvious the moment you wake up and primes the environment so the response of getting dressed requires zero friction.
